title: Living, perfused autologous replacements for complex parts that grafts do not supply

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a living replacement for a missing structural body part, made with the patient’s own cells, fabricated and implanted during one operation, and connected directly to the patient’s circulation. It would perform the missing part’s essential physical job immediately: carrying air or other contents, supporting weight, or closing a full-thickness body-wall defect. Candidate applications include a cervical tracheal segment, a weight-bearing long-bone segment, and an abdominal-wall replacement containing multiple tissue layers. Cells could be collected and prepared before the operation; the proposal does not require producing an expanded cell supply during surgery.

The defining combination is immediate blood supply, useful structural function, and sustained living tissue. Depositing cells at a defect, making a scaffold with the right shape, or creating vessels in a laboratory construct would each address part of the problem. The complete replacement would also need a vascular network that works after surgical connection, strength appropriate to its anatomical role, and integration with surrounding tissue. In situ bioprinting provides one relevant fabrication direction: the September 2026 robotic-bioprinting review describes depositing biomaterials, cells, and biological factors directly at defects. That direction does not itself establish the full replacement capability proposed here.

significance.text: If achieved, this capability would expand reconstruction by allowing an engineered living structure to take over a missing part’s conduit, barrier, or load-bearing function at surgery. It could reduce the need to transfer an existing functional tissue unit from elsewhere in the patient, subject to the requirements of each application. The advance would be the combination of surgical usability and living function: the replacement would have to survive while doing the physical work for which it was implanted. This is a proposed consequence of meeting the concept’s endpoints, rather than a reported clinical achievement.

Growth, adaptive remodeling, and resistance to infection are possible downstream benefits, but they would require separate demonstrations. Autologous cells, perfusion, and 90 days of structural function do not automatically establish any of those outcomes. Similarly, avoiding dependence on human donors would require a fabrication route that also avoids human donor scaffolds and other donor-derived components. Using the patient’s own cells establishes cell provenance; it does not establish the provenance or behavior of every material in the replacement.

The significance should not rest on an exhaustive claim that existing reconstruction offers only scar, transferred flaps, prostheses, or rare allografts. The supplied review identifies a 2014 FDA packet for a resorbable extracellular-matrix SIS Hernia Graft used in hernia or body-wall repair, illustrating an additional biological scaffold option. Such a packaged, dried scaffold is distinct from an immediately perfused autologous living replacement. Its existence narrows the account of what would be new without eliminating the proposed advance.

missing_breakthrough.text: A directly documented barrier is functional vascularization. The June 20, 2025 Nature Biomedical Engineering review identifies blood-vessel formation as a constraint on engineered-tissue survival and describes the need to organize vasculature across micrometre-to-millimetre scales. For this concept, a surgically connectable vessel would therefore need to serve a working network throughout the replacement. A connection that admits blood at one location would not alone demonstrate adequate perfusion of the living tissue.

Concept-specific engineering requirements include keeping that network open after surgical anastomosis, distributing flow sufficiently to maintain tissue viability, and preserving function during healing. The construct must also possess useful strength on day one: an airway must remain patent, a bone replacement must withstand its intended loads, and an abdominal wall must maintain a full-thickness barrier. These are proposed requirements of the replacement, not detailed failures established for every existing construct by the supplied review previews.

Integration introduces a further coupled problem. The replacement must join surrounding tissue while retaining the organization and mechanical behavior needed for its role, rather than being displaced by destructive scarring. Intraoperative fabrication must produce this combination within a usable surgical workflow, even if cells and other inputs are prepared beforehand. The supplied evidence does not quantify achievable fabrication times, immediate strength, or scar-related failure rates; those remain application-specific questions.

current_state.text: The September 14, 2026 ACS Biomaterials Science & Engineering review describes robotic in situ bioprinting as an early field, with studies largely confined to particular devices or isolated applications. Its retained abstract documents direct deposition at tissue defects as an active technical direction. It does not establish successful fabrication and implantation of a living, immediately functional structural replacement meeting this record’s proposed scope, nor does it provide a comprehensive account of every human application.

Two June 2025 reviews supply complementary context. The June 16 Nature Reviews Bioengineering review discusses clinical-translation challenges for solid organs engineered using decellularized scaffolds. The June 20 Nature Biomedical Engineering review identifies functional, multiscale vascularization as an engineered-tissue survival constraint. The supplied evidence review had access to abstracts or subscription previews for these conclusions. Those passages support the general translation and vascularization barriers, but do not establish the performance of all structural replacements.

The earlier research described laboratory constructs containing several cell types and vessels at centimetre scale. The retained material assessed in the supplied review does not establish those constructs’ dimensions, mechanical performance, or surgical use. The centimetre-scale statement therefore remains unverified in this record. The same evidence limitation prevents a categorical conclusion that no existing construct can provide immediate structural function or has been fabricated and joined during human surgery.

The research also attributed a statement about the absence of direct human in situ bioprinting to a February 9, 2026 Biofabrication review, originally encountered through a search index after a blocked publisher fetch. No retained text for that source was available to the supplied evidence review. Likewise, a July 26, 2025 Lancet review was said to describe recellularized liver or kidney tissues with basic organ functions, but its indexed summary and full text were not retained for verification. These attributions remain unresolved; the access gaps are not evidence that the reported statements or results are false.

None of the retained passages assessed in the supplied review reports a replacement satisfying the complete proposed milestone. This establishes an absence within that limited evidence set, not a field-wide absence as of November 1, 2026. The supplied record contains no bounded freshness search establishing comprehensive coverage to that date. Separately, the FDA SIS Hernia Graft packet retained alongside the Nature scaffold review is a different document; it supplies context about an existing scaffold option and cannot serve as the review’s full text or establish the field’s 2026 status.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed initial milestone: in a large animal, fabricate and implant an autologous living construct during one operation to replace a cervical tracheal segment, a weight-bearing long-bone segment, or a full-thickness abdominal wall. Cells may be prepared beforehand. The replacement should receive blood through a surgical anastomosis, perform the missing part’s conduit, load-bearing, or barrier function immediately, and maintain perfusion, tissue viability, and that function for at least 90 days without a permanent synthetic stent or prosthesis. Ninety days is a proposed milestone, not an established standard or proof of lifelong durability.
completion_criteria.label: Single-operation autologous replacement maintains perfusion, viability and function 90 days

completion_criteria.text: Proposed convincing evidence should document all three outcomes separately: continuing blood flow through the construct, survival of its living tissue, and performance of its intended structural role. Application-specific measurements should show airway patency and conduit function, load-bearing performance under stated conditions, or maintenance of the full-thickness body-wall barrier. Reporting should describe preparation time, intraoperative fabrication time, scaffold and cell provenance, temporary supports, complications, and any rescue procedures, so that the practical boundaries of the result are clear.
completion_criteria.label: Separate perfusion, viability and structural-function evidence includes practical limits

completion_criteria.text: A first human case meeting the same endpoints would constitute an initial clinical demonstration for that anatomical application. Repeated successes, preferably including independent reproduction, longer follow-up, and explicit reporting of failures would be needed to establish reliability and a broader clinical role. Success in one of the proposed anatomical alternatives would demonstrate that application; it would not establish successful replacement of all listed tissues. Finite testing can establish demonstrated breadth and durability under specified conditions, not universal applicability.
completion_criteria.label: Application-specific human success meets endpoints; reliability requires repeated successes

completion_criteria.text: A printed skin layer without vessels and mechanical integration would leave this scope unmet. Likewise, survival without useful structural function, temporary perfusion without sustained tissue viability, or function supplied by a permanent synthetic stent or prosthesis would not satisfy the proposed milestone. Growth, infection resistance, and complete independence from donor-derived materials should be evaluated as additional claims if pursued, rather than inferred from the core demonstration.
completion_criteria.label: Living tissue provides sustained structural function without permanent synthetic support

related_concepts.text: SUR-12, “Life-sustaining autologous solid organs assembled for implantation,” shares vascular engineering, cell sourcing, scaffolds, and surgical implantation with SUR-09. Its defining outcome is life-sustaining solid-organ function, such as that of a kidney, liver, or heart. SUR-09 instead targets structural conduit, barrier, or load-bearing function. Solving a structural replacement would not by itself demonstrate the physiological functions required for SUR-12.

SUR-02, “Destination-therapy solid-organ xenotransplantation,” addresses replacement through animal-derived organs and therefore a different supply route. SUR-01, “Operational donor-specific tolerance for the transplants patients actually receive,” addresses immune acceptance of donor transplants. SUR-09 proposes using the patient’s own cells, but any donor-derived scaffold or other component would still require its provenance and biological implications to be assessed. These concepts can share transplantation techniques without becoming the same achievement.

SUR-05, “Adult surgical wounds that heal by regeneration rather than fibrosis,” overlaps with the need for integration that preserves living structure instead of destructive scarring. Its central outcome concerns how a wound heals; SUR-09 concerns fabrication, perfusion, and immediate function of a replacement. Regenerative healing could improve a replacement’s durability, but neither capability alone establishes the other.

SUR-06, “Autonomous completion of whole operations at expert level,” SUR-07, “Incisionless resection and reconstruction inside the closed body,” and SUR-11, “Real-time cellular and molecular vision of the intact operative field,” could provide fabrication, delivery, anastomosis, or monitoring tools for a future replacement workflow. Their respective achievements concern operative autonomy, access, and sensing. SUR-09 requires a successful living replacement regardless of which tools are used to place or assess it.

change_log.change: Preserved SUR-09’s identity while making intraoperative fabrication, immediate structural function, and sustained living perfusion explicit.
change_log.reason: These jointly define the intended advance and distinguish it from cell deposition, scaffold placement, or vascularization alone.

change_log.change: Separated the documented multiscale vascularization barrier from proposed mechanical, surgical, and integration requirements.
change_log.reason: The retained vascular-patterning review supports the survival constraint but does not establish every detailed engineering assertion in the original text.

change_log.change: Retained the centimetre-scale construct assertion as unresolved rather than presenting it as established or deleting the concept.
change_log.reason: The supplied review could not verify the dimensions or performance from retained evidence; that limitation does not invalidate the replacement goal.

change_log.change: Qualified growth, infection resistance, and donor independence as additional conditional benefits.
change_log.reason: They do not follow automatically from autologous cells, perfusion, or 90-day structural function, and donor-derived scaffolds could remain part of fabrication.

change_log.change: Removed the exhaustive account of existing reconstructive substitutes and integrated the resorbable SIS Hernia Graft distinction.
change_log.reason: The supplied FDA packet demonstrates an additional scaffold option while describing a different capability from the proposed living replacement.

change_log.change: Preserved dated review findings while qualifying the Biofabrication and Lancet attributions and the November 2026 field-wide absence claim.
change_log.reason: Two sources lacked retained text, the accessible evidence was partial, and no bounded freshness search was supplied.

change_log.change: Used the supplied FDA resolved URL for the graft packet and kept it distinct from the Nature review.
change_log.reason: The packet was retained under the Nature source entry but is a separate 2014 device document.

change_log.change: Preserved the proposed 90-day milestone while narrowing a first human case to an initial demonstration for one application.
change_log.reason: One case and a finite follow-up interval cannot establish lifelong durability, reproducibility, general clinical readiness, or success across all listed tissues.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed verification and explained relevant roster overlaps without merging entries.
change_log.reason: Perfusion, viability, structural performance, practical constraints, and neighboring achievements need distinct evidence and boundaries.

unresolved_issues: The supplied retained evidence does not establish the dimensions, cell composition, immediate mechanical performance, or surgical use of the previously described centimetre-scale constructs.
The February 2026 Biofabrication statement about direct human in situ bioprinting remains unverified because no retained source text was available to the supplied review.
The July 2025 Lancet attribution concerning basic liver or kidney functions remains unverified because no retained source text was available.
Whether any qualifying human structural replacement existed by November 1, 2026 remains unresolved; the partial sources and empty freshness record cannot establish comprehensive absence.
Application-specific performance thresholds, acceptable temporary support, fabrication time, and follow-up beyond the proposed 90 days remain to be defined.
Growth, infection resistance, long-term integration, and independence from donor-derived materials require separate evidence.
The proposed large-animal and first-human milestones do not yet specify the replication needed to establish dependable clinical performance.

brief.title: Living body parts made from a patient's own cells
possible: Someone missing a section of windpipe, a weight-bearing bone or the full thickness of their abdominal wall could receive a living replacement made from their own cells. Surgeons would make and implant it during the same operation, connect it to the bloodstream and have it do its physical job immediately.
why: This would give reconstructive surgeons a way to replace missing structures while keeping the replacement tissue alive. It could reduce the need to move functioning tissue from elsewhere in the patient's body.

sources.showed: This review covers printing living materials directly at damaged tissue, including printing methods, materials and cell sources.
sources.cited_for: It discusses printing tissue directly where repair is needed.
sources.not_established: A review of printing approaches does not establish a living replacement that immediately performs a missing part's structural job.

sources.showed: Their review describes robots depositing cells and biological materials directly at tissue defects. It finds that studies remain largely confined to particular devices or isolated applications.
sources.quote: However, this field remains at an early stage, with existing studies largely limited to specific devices or isolated applications and lacking systematic reviews that compare diverse technological approaches.
sources.cited_for: Robotic tissue printing offers a fabrication route, but the field remains early.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate a replacement combining immediate blood supply, structural function and sustained tissue survival.

sources.showed: Their review describes using organs stripped of cells as supporting frameworks, then adding replacement cells. Large-animal organs can provide frameworks at human size.
sources.quote: Organs of large animals can be decellularized to create scaffolds for the engineering of human-sized organs.
sources.cited_for: Existing tissue frameworks offer another route to building replacement organs.
sources.not_established: A framework at human size does not establish a living structural replacement made and connected during surgery.

sources.showed: This review discusses advances in transplantable organs, including liver or kidney tissues repopulated with cells and described as having basic organ functions.
sources.cited_for: It provides context on rebuilding organ function with living cells.
sources.not_established: Basic liver or kidney functions do not establish immediate strength or a durable airway or body-wall barrier.

sources.showed: Their review identifies a working blood-vessel network as a constraint on engineered tissue survival. It describes the need to organize vessels from tiny branches to larger channels.
sources.quote: However, the survival of engineered tissues is constrained by the challenge of establishing a functional vasculature.
sources.cited_for: Blood must flow throughout the replacement to keep its tissue alive.
sources.not_established: Methods for arranging vessels do not establish sustained blood flow and structural function after surgical connection.

shown: Researchers have developed ways to print cells and biological materials directly at damaged tissue. Zitong Wang and colleagues describe an early field of device-specific studies and isolated applications. Tarek Saleh and colleagues describe organ frameworks made by removing existing cells, which can then receive replacement cells.
missing: A replacement would need a surgically connected vessel network that keeps blood flowing throughout its living tissue.
It would need useful strength immediately and retain its function while joining surrounding tissue during healing.
Fabrication and implantation would need to fit a practical operation, with preparation, supports, complications and rescue procedures documented.

milestones.label: A living replacement works for 90 days
milestones.explanation: A large-animal replacement made from its own cells during surgery would need immediate blood flow and function lasting 90 days. Replacing a neck windpipe segment, weight-bearing bone segment or full-thickness abdominal wall would qualify.

milestones.label: Blood flow, tissue survival and function are measured separately
milestones.explanation: Tests would need to measure blood flow, tissue survival and the replacement's physical job separately, alongside preparation, fabrication, materials, supports and complications. This would reveal what worked and its practical limits.

milestones.label: Human success becomes repeatable
milestones.explanation: A human case would need to meet the same endpoints, followed by repeated successes, preferably independently reproduced, with longer follow-up and failures reported. This would establish reliability for that particular body part.

milestones.label: Living tissue sustains function without permanent artificial support
milestones.explanation: Living tissue would need to sustain the structural job without a permanent synthetic brace or artificial replacement. This would establish that the tissue itself supplies the lasting function.

uncertain: The proposed 90-day target does not establish lifelong durability; suitable strength thresholds, temporary supports and longer follow-up remain undefined.
How many repeated successes would establish dependable clinical performance remains undecided.
Growth, infection resistance and freedom from donor-derived materials would each need separate demonstrations.
